# Introduction

In this analysis, I choose to work with Vacant or Abandoned Buildings Reported as the violation type. Given my interest in housing and economic development as well as having grown up in Chicago, I am curious to see where these reported violations occur and build a model that may be able to predict which areas of the city are likely to have vacant or abandoned buildings.

# Set Up


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

library(tidyverse)      # Data manipulation
library(sf)             # Spatial operations
library(here)           # Relative file paths
library(viridis)        # Color scales
library(terra)          # Raster operations (replaces 'raster')

library(FNN)            # Fast nearest neighbors
library(MASS)           # Negative binomial regression
library(patchwork)      # Plot composition (replaces grid/gridExtra)
library(knitr)          # Tables
library(kableExtra)     # Table formatting
library(classInt)       # Classification intervals


# Spatstat for analyzing point patterns - split into sub-packages
library(spatstat.geom)    # Spatial geometries
library(spatstat.explore) # Spatial exploration/KDE

# Set options
options(scipen = 999)  # No scientific notation
set.seed(5080)         # Reproducibility, could be any number

# Create consistent theme for visualizations
```

# Part 1: Data Loading and Exploration

## 1.1 Data Loading

Here, I am loading my 311 data and my Chicago spatial boundaries. I am loading in police districts, police beats, the Chicago city boundary, and vacant or abandoned buildings reported from 311 service requests downloaded from OpenData Chicago. I also do some basic data cleaning such as removing rows without coordinates and making the data spatial by transforming it using st_as_sf. I transformed all spatial layers to EPSG:3435 so they shared a common projected coordinate system appropriate for Chicago-area analysis.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Load police districts (used for spatial cross-validation)
policeDistricts <- 
  st_read("https://data.cityofchicago.org/api/geospatial/24zt-jpfn?method=export&format=GeoJSON") %>%
  st_transform(3435) %>%
  dplyr::select(District = dist_num)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# Load Vacant and Abandoned Buildings Reported Data from 311 Service Requests (open data)

         vacancy_status = 'IS THE BUILDING CURRENTLY VACANT OR OCCUPIED?')
```

::: callout-note
### Data Examination

There are **65,082** vacant or abandoned building service requests in the dataset. The dataset covers the time range from January 1, 2011 through December 31, 2017. I transformed this data into CRS 3435 (Illinois East State Plane) because it is designed specifically for the Chicago region, providing accurate distance and area measurements.
:::

## 1.2 Spatial Distribution

Next, I am creating visualizations to view the spatial distribution of vacant or abandoned buildings in Chicago. I am creating a simple point map, where each dot represents a vacant or abandoned building, and a density surface map to visualize any hot spots or clustering of these vacant/abandoned buildings.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Simple point map
p1 <- ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = chicagoBoundary, fill = "gray95", color = "gray60") +
  geom_sf(data = vacancies, color = "#d62828", size = 0.1, alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Vacant & Abandoned Buildings",
    subtitle = paste0("Chicago 2011-2017, n = ", nrow(vacancies))
  )

# Density surface using modern syntax
p2 <- ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = chicagoBoundary, fill = "gray95", color = "gray60") +
  geom_density_2d_filled(
    data = data.frame(st_coordinates(vacancies)),
    aes(X, Y),
    alpha = 0.7,
    bins = 8
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(
    option = "plasma",
    direction = -1,
    guide = "none"  # Modern ggplot2 syntax (not guide = FALSE)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Density Surface",
    subtitle = "Kernel density estimation"
  )


# Combine plots using patchwork (modern approach)
p1 + p2 + 
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Spatial Distribution of Vacant and Abandoned Buildings in Chicago",
    tag_levels = 'A'
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/visualizations-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


::: callout-note
### Spatial Distribution & Patterns

The simple point map of vacant and abandoned buildings shows that there are reports of these buildings throughout Chicago. Because there are so many data points, the the kernel density estimation map better visualizes spatial patterns of these reports. In the density surface map, a few hot spots emerge around the city, especially on the south side and slightly less on the west side, while there are no hot spots on the north side or downtown. This indicates a spatial pattern to vacant and abandoned buildings in Chicago. Chicago is a highly segregated city, and the south and west sides are generally home to larger concentrations of Black and Latine communities. The north side of the city has pockets of ethnic enclaves but is generally whiter and wealthier than the south and west sides of the city. This uneven spatial distribution likely reflects broader histories of disinvestment, segregation, and uneven neighborhood conditions across Chicago.
:::

# Part 2: Fishnet Grid Creation

## 2.1 Creating the Fishnet

Next, I am creating a fishnet grid.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 500 meters in feet
cell_size_ft <- 500 * 3.28084

fishnet <- st_make_grid(
  chicagoBoundary,
  cellsize = cell_size_ft,
  square = TRUE
) %>%
  st_sf() %>%
  mutate(uniqueID = row_number())

# Keep only cells that intersect Chicago
fishnet <- fishnet[chicagoBoundary, ]

cat("✓ Created fishnet grid\n")
```

# Part 3: Spatial Features

## 3.1 KDE Baseline


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Convert vacancy points to spatstat point pattern
vacancy_coords <- st_coordinates(vacancies)

vacancies_ppp <- ppp(
  x = vacancy_coords[, 1],
  y = vacancy_coords[, 2],
  window = as.owin(st_bbox(chicagoBoundary))
)

# KDE with 1 km bandwidth = 3280.84 feet
kde_vacancies <- density.ppp(
  vacancies_ppp,
  sigma = 3280.84,
  edge = TRUE
)

# Convert KDE to terra raster
kde_raster <- rast(kde_vacancies)

# Extract average KDE value to fishnet cells
fishnet$kde_value <- terra::extract(
  kde_raster,
  vect(fishnet),
  fun = mean,
  na.rm = TRUE
)[, 2]

cat("✓ Calculated KDE baseline\n")
```

## 3.2 k-Nearest Neighbor Features


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Get centroid coordinates for each fishnet cell
fishnet_centroids <- st_centroid(fishnet)
fishnet_coords <- st_coordinates(fishnet_centroids)

# Find 5 nearest neighboring cells for each cell
knn_5 <- get.knn(fishnet_coords, k = 5)

# Calculate mean vacancy count in neighboring cells
fishnet$vacancies_knn_mean <- purrr::map_dbl(1:nrow(fishnet), function(i) {
  neighbor_ids <- knn_5$nn.index[i, ]
  mean(fishnet$countVacancies[neighbor_ids], na.rm = TRUE)
})

summary(fishnet$vacancies_knn_mean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   0.00    3.80    9.80   26.89   32.35  266.20 
```


:::
:::


The k-nearest neighbor feature summarizes vacancy counts in nearby grid cells, capturing local spatial context. The distribution shows that while many areas have relatively low neighboring vacancy counts, some cells are surrounded by much higher levels of vacancy, indicating localized clustering. This variable helps the model account for spatial dependence, where vacancy reports in one location are influenced by nearby conditions.

## 3.3 Local Moran's I


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Create spatial weights from 5 nearest neighbors
coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(fishnet))
neighbors <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 5))
weights <- nb2listw(neighbors, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

# Calculate Local Moran's I on vacancy counts
local_moran <- localmoran(fishnet$countVacancies, weights)

# Mean count and spatial lag
mean_count <- mean(fishnet$countVacancies, na.rm = TRUE)
lag_count <- lag.listw(weights, fishnet$countVacancies, zero.policy = TRUE)

# Add results and classify clusters
fishnet <- fishnet %>%
  mutate(
    local_i = local_moran[, 1],
    p_value = local_moran[, 5],
    is_significant = p_value < 0.05,
    moran_class = case_when(
      !is_significant ~ "Not Significant",
      local_i > 0 & countVacancies > mean_count & lag_count > mean_count ~ "High-High",
      local_i > 0 & countVacancies <= mean_count & lag_count <= mean_count ~ "Low-Low",
      local_i < 0 & countVacancies > mean_count & lag_count <= mean_count ~ "High-Low",
      local_i < 0 & countVacancies <= mean_count & lag_count > mean_count ~ "Low-High",
      TRUE ~ "Not Significant"
    )
  )
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = fishnet, aes(fill = moran_class), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "High-High" = "#d7191c",
      "High-Low" = "#fdae61",
      "Low-High" = "#abd9e9",
      "Low-Low" = "#2c7bb6",
      "Not Significant" = "gray90"
    ),
    name = "Cluster Type"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Local Moran's I: Vacancy Report Clusters",
    subtitle = "High-High cells indicate hot spots of vacancy reports"
  ) +
  theme_vacant()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The Local Moran’s I results identify clusters of vacant building reports concentrated primarily on the South and West sides of Chicago. These high-high clusters indicate areas where high vacancy counts are surrounded by similarly high neighboring counts, suggesting strong spatial concentration. This pattern reinforces earlier observations that vacancy reports are not randomly distributed but instead occur in localized hot spots across the city.

## 3.4 Distance to Hot Spots


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hotspots <- fishnet %>%
  filter(moran_class == "High-High") %>%
  st_centroid()

if (nrow(hotspots) > 0) {
  fishnet <- fishnet %>%
    mutate(
      dist_to_hotspot = as.numeric(
        st_distance(st_centroid(fishnet), hotspots %>% st_union())
      )
    )

  cat("✓ Calculated distance to vacancy-report hot spots\n")
  cat("  - Number of hot spot cells:", nrow(hotspots), "\n")
} else {
  fishnet <- fishnet %>%
    mutate(dist_to_hotspot = 0)

  cat("⚠ No significant hot spots found\n")
}
```


## Summary

Both Poisson and Negative Binomial regression results show that neighboring vacancy levels and distance to hot spots are statistically significant predictors of vacancy counts. The positive coefficient for the k-nearest neighbor variable suggests that areas surrounded by higher vacancy counts tend to have more vacancy reports, while the negative distance coefficient indicates that vacancy counts decrease farther from hot spots. The large overdispersion value (14.3) indicates that the Poisson model is inappropriate, and the Negative Binomial model provides a better fit, as reflected by the substantially lower AIC.

## 5.3 Leave-One-Group-Out Cross-Validation


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# LOGO CV with negative binomial
districts <- unique(fishnet_cv_model$District)
cv_results <- tibble()

cat("Running LOGO Cross-Validation...\n")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Running LOGO Cross-Validation...
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
for (i in seq_along(districts)) {

  test_district <- districts[i]

  train_data <- fishnet_cv_model %>% filter(District != test_district)
  test_data  <- fishnet_cv_model %>% filter(District == test_district)

  model_cv <- glm.nb(
    countVacancies2017 ~ vacancies_knn_mean + dist_to_hotspot,
    data = train_data
  )

  test_data <- test_data %>%
    mutate(
      prediction = predict(model_cv, test_data, type = "response")
    )

  mae <- mean(abs(test_data$countVacancies2017 - test_data$prediction))
  rmse <- sqrt(mean((test_data$countVacancies2017 - test_data$prediction)^2))

  cv_results <- bind_rows(
    cv_results,
    tibble(
      fold = i,
      test_district = test_district,
      n_test = nrow(test_data),
      mae = mae,
      rmse = rmse
    )
  )

  cat("  Fold", i, "/", length(districts), "- District", test_district,
      "- MAE:", round(mae, 2), "\n")
}
```

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot() +

  geom_sf(data = chicagoBoundary, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
```

The error map shows that the model performs well across most of Chicago, with relatively low prediction errors in many grid cells. However, larger errors are concentrated in parts of the South and West sides, where vacant building reports appear to be more clustered and variable. This suggests that while the spatial predictors capture broad patterns, additional neighborhood-level factors may be needed to better predict vacancy concentrations in these high-variability areas.

## Evaluation

To evaluate model performance, I compared the spatial regression model to a KDE baseline. The regression model achieved lower MAE and RMSE values than the KDE baseline, indicating improved predictive accuracy. This suggests that incorporating spatial features such as nearest neighbor vacancy counts and distance to hot spots improves predictive performance beyond simple spatial smoothing. However, errors remain higher in certain areas of the city, particularly in neighborhoods with highly clustered vacancy patterns, suggesting additional predictors may further improve model performance.
